solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Returning explorer in charge of filling ship: a cutter

definitions.note: the answer is a plural-form noun for a single tool

indicators.note: something returning comes back the way it went, so the letters run backwards
a filling sits inside something else, so these letters go within the ship

blocks.note: James Clark Ross, the polar explorer

explanation.surface: A naval explorer heading home has command of a vessel that is itself a cutter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutter' looks like a type of boat, matching the ship, but here it is a cutting tool. James Clark Ross explored both polar regions.
explanation.definitionFit: Scissors is a cutting implement, so it is fairly described as a cutter even though grammatically plural.

clue.text: Drop jokes etc, almost all personal

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is cut off

blocks.note: jokes and the like make comedy
one's own is all one's personal property

explanation.surface: Someone's jokes fall flat, almost all of them personal ones.
explanation.definitionFit: A comedown is a fall in status or a disappointing decline, so a drop.

clue.text: No good for wife of brother to display fortitude

indicators.note: for means in place of, so one item is swapped in where the other stood

blocks.note: both are exclamations of surprise or dismay, as in 'Oh brother!'
NG is short for no good

explanation.surface: A brother's wife is no good at showing courage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wife of brother' looks like a sister-in-law, but 'brother' is the exclamation, matching the old oath STREWTH, whose W gives way to NG.
explanation.definitionFit: Strength of character is fortitude, the courage to endure hardship.

clue.text: Kilometre trails go from suburbs, always ending in city

indicators.note: each word always contributes its ending, its last letter
trailing means following behind, so the kilometre letter comes last

blocks.note: the last letter of each word

explanation.surface: Commuter trails stretch for a kilometre from the suburbs into town.
explanation.definitionFit: Omsk is a large city in south-western Siberia, Russia.

clue.text: Moslem, I hesitate to say, is more cheerful

blocks.note: a Sunni is a member of the larger branch of Islam

explanation.surface: A hesitant speaker suggests a Muslim is in better spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunny in mood means bright and cheerful, and this is its comparative form.

clue.text: Skin blemish to be somehow acceptable, we note down here?

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters are arranged differently

blocks.note: a pock is a pustule or pit in the skin
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a skin spot is fine and whether to record it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition describes the thing by its use, hence the question mark; in American English the word also means a handbag.
explanation.definitionFit: A small notebook carried in the pocket is where one jots notes down.

clue.text: Popular expectation, ultimately wild all round, is confounded

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is wanted
a word that is all round another surrounds it

explanation.surface: A widely held expectation is wrecked by something wild.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are mild intensifying curses meaning damned, as in a confounded nuisance.

clue.text: Sticking poster chap has torn

blocks.note: rent is an old past tense of rend, to tear

explanation.surface: A man has torn down a poster that was stuck up.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means clinging or sticking fast to something.

clue.text: Sealed informal refusal to stop nude rambling

indicators.note: to stop a gap is to plug it, so this word is put into the middle of the other letters
rambling wanders all over the place, so the letters of nude are disordered

blocks.note: a casual way of saying no
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone says a casual no to stop a naked person wandering about.
explanation.walkthrough: The insertion goes after the first letter of the rearranged word, not at its centre.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sealed has not been opened yet, so the two adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: One's certainly not quietly reflecting — give time to?

indicators.note: a reflection shows a mirror image, so the words for certainly not are read backwards

blocks.note: one is, from the speaker's viewpoint I'm
P is piano, the musical direction for softly

explanation.surface: Someone thinks about whether they are certainly not keeping quiet, and asks about giving time.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on 'giving time' as a jail sentence, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A judge who gives someone time sentences them to a spell in jail, which is to lock them up.

clue.text: Need a key to set loose helpless viewer

indicators.note: letters set loose are freed from their order and can fall into a new one

explanation.surface: You need a key to free a prisoner who cannot see or help themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: The unaided eye looks without any telescope or microscope, so it is a viewer without help.

clue.text: Most daring to draw on money, then skint on vacation

indicators.note: in a down-free across clue, one thing placed on another follows it in the reading order
a place on vacation is emptied, so only the outer letters remain

blocks.note: a drawn match is a tie

explanation.surface: Someone broke has to borrow money, and is told they must be very bold.
explanation.walkthrough: Skint is British slang for having no money, which fits the surface's borrowing.
explanation.definitionFit: Doughty means brave and valiant, so its superlative is the bravest or most daring.

clue.text: One turned agonisingly from gang after attempts to get picked up

indicators.note: after places the gang word behind the other one in reading order

explanation.surface: Someone agonisingly turned away from a gang after trying to hitch a ride.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a torture device that is tightened by turning, crushing the victim's thumbs.
explanation.definitionFit: This old instrument of torture is a screw turned to cause agony.

clue.text: I would catch cold: never again?

indicators.note: to catch something is to hold it, so the cold letter goes inside

blocks.note: the Roman numeral I is one
C is the abbreviation for cold on taps

explanation.surface: Someone says they would catch a cold and vows not to do that a second time.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is by example: something done only once is never done again, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something only a single time means it happens just one occasion and not again afterwards.

clue.text: Heading for success within month: euphoric!

indicators.note: within says the answer is lying inside the run of words that follows

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: Someone thrilled with how things have gone this month says they are on track to succeed.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a person or business whose fortunes are improving and rising.

clue.text: Least intelligent pupil previously useless in exam

indicators.note: in says one item is placed inside another

blocks.note: an old boy is a former pupil
U/S is short for unserviceable, useless

explanation.surface: A pupil who did badly in a test earlier is the dimmest.
explanation.definitionFit: Obtuse means slow to understand, so the superlative is the dullest or least clever.

clue.text: His return now would make him wealthier? Or poorer?

definitions.text: His return now would make him wealthier? Or poorer?

blocks.clueFragment: His return now would make him wealthier?
blocks.note: surface reading: a puzzle about someone whose coming home changes his fortune
setter's reading: a person who lives abroad to avoid tax; his tax return now is light, but returning home would cost him

explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' works twice: the tax form he files abroad keeps him rich, while a return home would make him pay up.
explanation.definitionFit: A wealthy person living overseas to escape high taxes at home is exactly the person described.

clue.text: Policeman, one with crowd, giving help to direct

definitions.note: the answer is a noun, a person who helps to direct

blocks.note: a lot is a group or crowd

explanation.surface: An officer alongside a throng helps with traffic direction.
explanation.definitionFit: A second pilot assists the captain in flying and steering an aircraft.

clue.text: Saw with difficulty through this unusual, frameless "door-window"?

indicators.note: without a frame means the outside edges are removed
unusual means not in the normal form, so the remaining letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Sawing through an odd door-window without its frame is hard work.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing the outer D and W leaves eight letters to rearrange. The definition describes a timber by how hard it is to saw.
explanation.definitionFit: Ironwood is any of several trees with extremely hard, dense timber that resists cutting.

clue.text: He passed on one note out of habit?

blocks.note: obiit, Latin for he died, abbreviated on gravestones

explanation.surface: A dead monk with a single remark has given up wearing his habit.
explanation.walkthrough: Habit here means custom or usage rather than a monk's robe; something no longer in use is out of habit.
explanation.definitionFit: Something obsolete has fallen out of use or custom.

clue.text: Reveal cricketer has time for golf

indicators.note: has time for golf means one letter is given in place of the other

blocks.note: leg slip is a fielding position near the batsman on the leg side
G is golf in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A cricketer reveals he swaps cricket for golf in his spare time.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a fielder is named after his position, so a leg slip is a cricketer.
explanation.definitionFit: To let slip is to reveal something, usually accidentally.

clue.text: Message of note by journalist's ending

indicators.note: an ending is the final part, so only the last letter of the journalist's word is wanted

blocks.note: te is a note of the sol-fa scale
by as in multiplication, the times sign
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A short message written by a reporter at the close of their piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' gives X because three by four means three times four.
explanation.definitionFit: A text is a message sent by mobile phone.

clue.text: Each week, finally husband wears shirt for work with suit

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the preceding word
something worn is wrapped around, so the shirt goes around the other letters

explanation.surface: Every week a husband dons a shirt to go with his office suit.
explanation.walkthrough: The suit is a lawsuit: Dickens's novel turns on the endless case of Jarndyce and Jarndyce.
explanation.definitionFit: This Dickens novel is a literary work built around an interminable Chancery lawsuit.

clue.text: Muscles displayed by four dozen rugby players

blocks.note: second meaning: a rugby union pack is eight forwards, and six of them make forty-eight

explanation.surface: A large squad of rugby players shows off its muscles.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby union the pack is the eight forwards, so six packs are four dozen players.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is slang for toned stomach muscles and literally six groups of rugby forwards.

clue.text: Sound made by small hole in bucket

indicators.note: the sound made by a word is what you hear when it is said

blocks.note: a pore is a tiny opening in the skin

explanation.surface: A small hole in a bucket makes a noise as water drips out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bucket' looks like a pail with a hole, but it is a verb: to bucket down is to rain heavily. In British speech the two words sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: When rain pours, it is bucketing down, falling in torrents.

clue.text: Appear to have finished scan

blocks.note: to look a certain way is to appear so

explanation.surface: Someone appears to have completed a scan.
explanation.definitionFit: To scan a document is to examine or glance through it, the same as this phrasal verb.

clue.text: Island's legal system blocking appeals by one

indicators.note: something blocking a passage sits inside it, so the legal letters go within

explanation.surface: An island's courts obstruct appeals from a single person.
explanation.walkthrough: Sue here is the old sense of to plead or petition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sulawesi, once called Celebes, is a large island of Indonesia.

clue.text: Multicoloured trousers a boy took off

indicators.note: used as a verb, to trouser is to pocket, so these letters hold the others inside

explanation.surface: A lad removed his brightly coloured trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' looks like clothing the boy took off, but it is a verb meaning pockets; take off means mimic.
explanation.definitionFit: To take someone off is to impersonate or mimic them, which is what a parody does.
